x.A: KMS customer managed keys are managed in AWS, so the encryption keys wouldn't be managed outside the AWS Cloud.
x.B: An AWS managed key is created and managed by AWS, so it isn't managed outside AWS.

x.D: Encrypting the data at the company's data center with its own keys before uploading over HTTPS keeps the keys outside AWS, and the data is encrypted in transit (TLS) and at rest in S3.

x.A: EKS Anywhere runs Kubernetes on premises, which means managing infrastructure, and EventBridge rules can't validate payloads.
x.B: EKS with self-managed nodes means managing the nodes, which is more infrastructure management, and Step Functions adds an unneeded layer for basic validation.
x.C: Spot Instances and a Spot Fleet mean managing servers, and Spot Instances can be interrupted during long-running processing.
x.D: API Gateway and Lambda validate the notifications with no servers, and ECS on Fargate runs the long-running backend with CPU and memory you can adjust and no infrastructure to manage.

x.A: Cognito user pools scale to millions of users, and their adaptive authentication feature calls for MFA when it detects risk, such as an unusual location, IP address, or device.
x.B: Identity pools provide AWS credentials and don't authenticate users with risk-based MFA.
x.C: IAM users don't scale to millions of users, and the AllowManageOwnUserMFA action just lets users manage MFA.
x.D: IAM Identity Center is for workforce access to AWS accounts and applications, and doesn't have risk-based adaptive authentication for millions of customers.

x.A: EMR is not serverless, so running a daily EMR job means managing clusters.
x.B: EMR isn't serverless, and Aurora isn't an MPP data warehouse.
x.C: A Glue job is serverless and transforms the data, Redshift Serverless is an MPP data warehouse, and Redshift ML lets analysts create and train ML models with SQL.
x.D: Athena is a query service, not an MPP data warehouse, and Athena doesn't have ML model training with SQL like Redshift ML.

x.A: Local Zones are AWS infrastructure in metro areas, not something placed in the company's own data center.
x.B: Snowmobile is a data transfer truck and doesn't run EKS locally.
x.C: An Outposts rack brings AWS infrastructure and services like EKS into the company's data center, so data stays on premises and the company can use AWS managed services.
x.D: Snowball Edge Storage Optimized is for storing and transferring data and isn't meant to run EKS as a long-term local environment.

x.A: A Volume Gateway presents block storage (iSCSI), but the data is on NFS storage, so a file interface is needed.
x.B: An S3 File Gateway presents NFS file shares backed by S3, so the existing workloads can keep using NFS. An S3 Lifecycle policy moves older data to cheaper classes, which is cost-effective and scalable.
x.C: EFS Standard-IA is more expensive than S3 for large amounts of data, and the workloads would need to access EFS over the network.
x.D: EFS One Zone-IA costs more than S3 and has less resilience.

x.A: Reserved concurrency limits the maximum and doesn't improve latency, and decreasing memory reduces CPU for CPU-intensive code, so processing takes longer.
x.B: Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory, so raising memory by Compute Optimizer's recommendation speeds up CPU-intensive code, reducing duration and cost while maintaining latency. Reserved concurrency guarantees capacity for the functions.
x.C: Provisioned concurrency costs extra, and lowering memory slows CPU-intensive code.
x.D: Provisioned concurrency adds cost all the time, which doesn't reduce compute cost.

x.A: ECR scan on push automatically scans each new image for CVEs, and ECS can pull from ECR, so only the image repository changes. It's the fewest changes.
x.B: Macie finds sensitive data in S3 and doesn't scan container images for CVEs.
x.C: Moving to EKS is a big change, and the question asks for the fewest changes to the workloads.
x.D: Inspector doesn't scan images stored in S3, and the Lambda approach is more custom work.

x.A: An EventBridge rule matches Batch job SUCCEEDED events, and an API destination calls the third-party HTTP API with basic (username and password) authentication, with no servers or code.
x.B: EventBridge Scheduler runs on schedules and doesn't match events, and a Lambda function adds code.
x.C: A Batch job can't publish events to API Gateway on its own in this design. EventBridge already receives Batch state change events.
x.D: This also needs Batch to publish to API Gateway, plus a Lambda function with custom code.

x.A: A Direct Connect hosted connection and VPC peering don't give the company's VPC access to the vendor's RDS database, because the company has no on-premises network and peering needs overlapping setup across accounts.
x.B: A client VPN connects users to a VPC and doesn't connect two VPCs.
x.C: The vendor puts an NLB in front of the RDS database and exposes it as a PrivateLink endpoint service. The company's VPC connects privately with an interface endpoint, with no internet gateway, VPN, or Direct Connect.
x.D: A transit gateway plus peering doesn't make sense together, and it exposes more of the vendor's network than needed.

x.A: A workspace without a VPC and a public RDS endpoint exposes the data over the internet.
x.B: A Managed Grafana workspace in a VPC can reach the RDS database over its private endpoint, so the data isn't exposed to the internet.
x.C: PrivateLink isn't how a workspace without a VPC connects to RDS.
x.D: A public RDS endpoint exposes the database over the internet, even if the workspace is in a VPC.

x.A: Glue Studio is visual but needs you to build and share jobs, and it doesn't provide data profiling and lineage in a no-code recipe format as DataBrew does.
x.B: EMR Serverless needs code to transform the data.
x.C: Glue DataBrew is a no-code data preparation tool with built-in transformations, data profiling, and lineage, and recipes can be shared across the company.
x.D: Athena SQL queries are code, and they don't provide data profiling and lineage.

x.A: An A record (alias) for the development site points to the ALB, and a listener rule forwards requests for the development host name to the target group with the development instance. If the instance is replaced, the target group registration keeps routing to it.
x.B: A public IP address on the instance changes when it's replaced, so the DNS record would break, and it exposes the instance directly.
x.C: The ALB can't redirect to a public IP in this way, and a redirect would break if the instance is replaced.
x.D: Putting all instances in one target group means the development host name could be routed to any instance, not only the development instance.

x.A: SQS doesn't support the AMQP protocol, so the application would need to be changed.
x.B: EKS runs the Kubernetes workloads with minimal changes, and Amazon MQ supports AMQP, so the application keeps its messaging code. Both are managed services.
x.C: EC2 instances mean managing servers and the container platform, which is more overhead.
x.D: Lambda and SQS would need the application to be rewritten, and SQS doesn't support AMQP.

x.A: ALBs don't improve end-to-end load time across Regions and work only with HTTP and HTTPS, so they could break the game traffic.
x.B: Weighted routing splits traffic evenly regardless of the user's location, which doesn't reduce latency.
x.C: More NLBs and instances in other Regions cost a lot and take work, and users still need to be routed to the closest one.
x.D: A Global Accelerator standard accelerator routes users over the AWS global network to the closest healthy NLB endpoint, which reduces end-to-end latency for global players.

x.A: DMS replicates databases and isn't an SFTP endpoint for vendors to upload files.
x.B: AWS Transfer Family provides a managed SFTP endpoint that stores files in S3, so the vendors keep using their SFTP-based applications, and the company has no servers to run.
x.C: An SFTP server on EC2 means managing the server, so it has more operational overhead.
x.D: S3 File Gateway presents an SMB or NFS share and runs as a gateway to manage, which doesn't support SFTP.

x.A: Athena queries structured data with SQL, but it doesn't analyze content and sentiment of text.
x.B: Building a sentiment model with SageMaker needs ML expertise and more operational work than using a managed NLP service.

x.A: Kinesis Data Streams ingests the real-time data, and Firehose delivers it to the S3 bucket as raw data. Both are managed and scale automatically.

x.D: Direct Connect isn't needed for ingestion, and the third-party applications would need to write directly to Firehose with PUT operations, which isn't specified.

x.A: Filtering with Lambda and storing in DocumentDB adds a second database to manage, which is more operational work.
x.B: DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, so large data goes to S3 and the DynamoDB item keeps the S3 URL. S3 scales without limit, and it's a well-known, low-effort pattern.
x.C: Splitting items by the same partition key gets around item size but adds complex code to rebuild the data, and BatchWriteItem isn't atomic.
x.D: Compressing with gzip might not bring items under 400 KB as the data keeps growing, and it adds processing.
